reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes deploying and funding a custom contract to perform an alleged arbitrage strategy while presenting a rapid return from about $200 to $1,775 as a successful result. The speaker instructs viewers to send AVAX to the contract, calls the process an arbitrage attack, and encourages them to spread the word and stack it, making the content an active solicitation rather than neutral financial education.

deploying Contract/Token to mask our arbitrage attack against Pangolin

opening.argument: Judge, the creator presents this as a personal experiment, not a dependable return for viewers: “This worked for me” is immediately followed by an explicit warning to try it at their own risk. The description also identifies AVAX as a cost required to run the process, rather than concealing that viewers would have to commit funds. The reported gain may be questionable, but a claimed personal result plus an express risk warning does not, by itself, establish a promise that others will profit.

citations.quote: This worked for me. But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK.
NEW GAS FEE REQUIRED: APPROX 10.5 AVAX

rebuttal.rebuttal: The quoted $200-to-$1,775 claim is emphatic, but it reports what the speaker says happened, not a stated guarantee for every viewer. The description's risk warning is material context for interpreting that claim. Likewise, creating and funding a token may be risky, but the quoted steps alone do not establish that the creator receives viewers' funds.

citations.quote: so we went $200 to 1775 dollars
But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A warning does not neutralize the concrete invitation to fund the contract. The instructions tell viewers to send AVAX to it and call the flash-loan function, while the speaker celebrates a dramatic return and urges viewers to act while they can. That combination promotes a funded-contract profit workflow regardless of whether the return is phrased as a universal guarantee.

opening.argument: Judge, the video's structure is a technical walkthrough. The speaker says the purpose is to explain how the process works, then walks through creating a Solidity file, choosing a compiler, connecting MetaMask to Remix, and deploying a contract. The description provides sequential setup instructions and links to flash-loan background material. A viewer can reasonably read the reported result as part of that demonstration, not as proof that every viewer is being offered an investment return.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening treats instruction as solicitation. Yet its quoted account of creating a token and funding it is also the subject the speaker says he is explaining. The profit claim deserves scrutiny, but the presence of a result in a step-by-step demonstration does not alone settle whether the video's primary purpose is deceptive recruitment.

citations.quote: So how this actually works, so that you all understand, is that we are creating our own Coin or Token on-chain.
so we went $200 to 1775 dollars

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technical walkthrough is the means of promotion, not a separate educational exercise. It gives viewers an executable sequence culminating in sending AVAX to the contract, then pairs that sequence with a striking claimed profit. Calling the steps a demonstration does not explain away the instruction to fund the contract.

so we went $200 to 1775 dollars fuck yeah spread the word don't spread too much though, but stack it while you can guys.

opening.argument: Judge, the funding instruction is specifically for a contract the viewer deploys and whose address the viewer obtains in Remix. The speaker also says that even a token with the same name as his would have a separate on-chain hash. Those details matter: the supplied instructions do not identify a creator-controlled payment address, request wallet credentials, or describe commissions for recruiting others. The mechanism actually described is deploying and operating a contract. Its safety and profitability are unverified, but the quoted funding step does not establish that viewers are paying the creator.

citations.quote: On Deploy, Enter your token details and deploy the contract 5. Get the Contract address from Remix 6. Send $200 of Avalanche/AVAX to the contract for gas fee
You can even name it the same as mine. It will have a separate hash on chain.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening correctly notes a funded contract and a claimed gain. It does not show where that contract sends funds or establish that the speaker controls the address viewers would fund. The quoted instruction has viewers obtain an address from their own Remix deployment. Without inspecting the contract's behavior, a funding requirement and an implausible-sounding result are concerns, not proof of the particular transfer mechanism alleged.

citations.quote: Get the Contract address from Remix 6. Send $200 of Avalanche/AVAX to the contract for gas fee
so we went $200 to 1775 dollars

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A creator-controlled destination need not be visible for this content to promote a risky funded-contract returns scheme. Viewers are explicitly told to deploy code from a supplied link, transfer AVAX to the resulting contract, and invoke a function; the video then presents a rapid, large profit as the outcome. A distinct contract address does not establish that its code protects the viewer's funds.
